Arizona.lede: {STATE}'s $166,988,956 Rural Health Transformation Program award — the plan, the three administering agencies, the budget split, live procurements, with a dated log of official activity.

answers.html: Arizona received $166,988,956 in Year 1 funding under CMS Notice of Award RHTCMS332059-01-00, dated December 29, 2025, with a five-year period of performance running through October 30, 2030. The award is Arizona's share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program.
answers.text: Arizona received $166,988,956 in Year 1 funding under CMS Notice of Award RHTCMS332059-01-00 (Dec 29, 2025), with a five-year period of performance through October 30, 2030 — its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program.

answers.html: AHCCCS (the Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System) is the single CMS awardee. The Governor's Office named three lead agencies to administer distinct slices: the Office of Economic Opportunity (OEO) runs workforce; the Department of Health Services (ADHS) runs maternal health and chronic-disease work; and AHCCCS runs everything else. Program coordination runs through the Arizona Center for Rural Health (manand@arizona.edu).
answers.text: AHCCCS is the single CMS awardee. The Governor's Office named three lead agencies: OEO (workforce), ADHS (maternal and chronic disease), and AHCCCS (everything else). Coordination runs through the Arizona Center for Rural Health (manand@arizona.edu).

answers.html: Arizona is using RHTP dollars to strengthen the rural health workforce, expand access through telehealth, mobile care and satellite sites, and make rural providers financially and operationally resilient through diagnostic equipment, EHR modernization and shared-services consortiums — coordinated across three state agencies rather than a single office.
answers.text: Arizona is using RHTP dollars to strengthen the rural workforce, expand access via telehealth/mobile/satellite care, and make rural providers resilient through equipment, EHR modernization and shared services — coordinated across three agencies.

answers.html:
• Rural Health Education & Training (OEO) — 28% (≈$47M), the single largest slice.

  • Making Rural Health Care Accessible (AHCCCS) — 23% (telehealth/digital 10%, rural-health innovation 13%).

answers.html:
Eligibility runs on two tracks. Direct-to-state contracts go out as competitive RFPs, where firms bid as prime contractors. Subgrants and subawards flow to rural providers — hospitals, Rural Health Clinics, FQHCs, Tribal health organizations, EMS agencies, counties and fire districts — and it is here that technology vendors and consultants most often engage as subcontractors or implementation partners rather than as direct grantees.

Track opportunities on the AHCCCS RHTP hub and the Grants Administration portal; attend the regional “Share Your Voice” meetings to shape priorities before more solicitations drop; and request a letter of support from the Arizona Center for Rural Health (as State Office of Rural Health) by sending them a link to an open funding opportunity.

answers.html: Alabama's Year-1 budget under the Alabama Rural Health Transformation Program (ARHTP) is approximately $203.4 million, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program — 100% CMS/HHS-funded. CMS structures the program over five years, and Alabama's approved narrative pairs Year-1 estimates with larger five-year totals for each initiative (for example, Collaborative EHR/IT/Cybersecurity shows $31.6M in Year 1 against a $125M five-year total).

answers.html: Alabama's strategy moves beyond short-term stabilization toward long-term system redesign, built around Regional Referral Center Hubs — larger regional hospitals or health systems that serve as central resource points for smaller rural providers, offering shared IT, cybersecurity, and specialty telehealth while letting independent providers keep their autonomy. The state identified 11 interrelated initiatives, 10 of which launch in Year 1 (the Community Medicine Initiative is deferred to Year 2).

Alaska.lede: Alaska's roughly $272.2 million Rural Health Transformation Program award — the plan, the administering agency, the six initiative tracks, the Letter-of-Interest pipeline, with a dated log of official activity.

answers.html: Alaska's Budget Period 1 award is approximately $272.2 million, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program and among the largest per-capita awards in the country. Arkansas.lede: Arkansas's $208.8M Rural Health Transformation Program award — the “Healthy. Connected. Local” plan, its four initiative tracks, live NOFOs, with a dated log of official activity for vendors, providers, and consultants tracking the program.

answers.html: Arkansas's FY2026 allocation is approximately $208.8 million (reported by the state as roughly $209 million), its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. CMS structures the program over five years; Arkansas's initiatives carry both Year-1 ceilings and larger five-year totals (its HEART pillar, for example, is about $27.6M in Year 1 against roughly $151.9M over five years), and — per CMS rules — every Year-1 dollar must be obligated by October 30, 2026.

answers.html: Arkansas structures its award into four named initiative tracks that together modernize the rural health system: PACT (Promoting Access, Coordination, and Transformation) for access, coordinated care, and clinically integrated networks; THRIVE (Telehealth, Health-Monitoring, and Response Innovation for Vital Expansion) for telehealth, remote patient monitoring, and EMS/emergency response; RISE AR (Recruitment, Innovation, Skills, and Education) for workforce and leadership; and HEART (Healthy Eating, Active Recreation, and Transformation) for prevention, nutrition, and chronic-disease work. No matching funds are required on these tracks.

answers.html:
Eligibility runs on two tracks. Direct-to-state contracts go out as competitive RFAs, where firms bid as prime contractors — and California's is unusually open: out-of-state organizations can apply directly with no California partner required, as long as they can meet state contracting requirements and deliver services in rural California, and "rural serving" is keyed to who benefits (per the HRSA Rural Health Grants Eligibility Analyzer), not where the applicant sits. Subawards flow to rural providers — CAHs, FQHCs (including Tribal), Rural Health Clinics, health care districts and county behavioral-health sites — where vendors and consultants engage as subcontractors or implementation partners. Note two limits: county public health departments cannot be primary recipients (only State-selected partners or subrecipients), and broadband expansion is not permissible.

Track opportunities on the CalRHT funding page, join the HCAI mailing list, and email a resume and expression of interest to CalRHT@hcai.ca.gov to be considered for the Rural Health Policy Council.

answers.html:
Florida's plan pushes care beyond traditional clinical walls — mobile health units, community paramedicine, remote patient monitoring, pharmacy-based retail clinics, satellite clinics and telehealth — while strengthening rural facilities' capacity for specialty and acute care, workforce pipelines, and value-based purchasing. A load-bearing technology thread is Florida HIE/ENS onboarding: the plan targets raising EHR and diagnostic interoperability among rural facilities from a 2024 baseline of about 73% to at least 83% by FY2030. Key project tags include Satellite Clinic Expansion, Mobile Maternal and Pharmacy Tech.

Florida structured its Year-1 funding as two bundled RFAs plus four standalone RFAs:

  • Preventive Care & Care-at-Home Bundle (RFA 033-25/26) — five integrated initiatives (mobile units, community paramedicine, remote telemonitoring, pharmacy retail clinics, mandatory Florida HIE connectivity).
  • Specialty & Acute Care Bundle (RFA 034-25/26) — HIE integration, diagnostic support, and a lead telehealth initiative (specialty, eICU, telestroke, or behavioral health).
  • Value-Based Purchasing (RFA 035-25/26), Initiative 11.
  • Rural Satellite Clinics (RFA 036-25/26), Initiative 1.
  • Workforce Development (RFA 037-25/26), Initiative 8.
  • Health & Lifestyle (RFA 038-25/26), Initiative 9.

The full breakdown is in Florida's budget narrative.

answers.html: Idaho organizes its plan around five initiatives: (1) improving rural access to care through technology — facility technology assessments, telehealth, digital health, cybersecurity and AI tools, emergency communications, data analytics and EHR upgrades; (2) innovative care-delivery models — diagnostic and care-access innovations, health extenders, and EMS expansion; (3) sustaining the rural workforce through ladder payments, career pathways, work-based learning and graduate medical education; (4) population-specific, evidence-based projects in chronic disease, behavioral health, and maternal and child health; and (5) rural health infrastructure and partnerships — facility renovations, pharmacy solutions, clinical equipment, patient-transport vehicles, safety-code compliance and Tribal support. The five initiatives contemplate roughly 23 targeted procurements.

answers.html: The single largest Year 1 vehicle is an $83,700,800 competitive subgrant pool for technology, equipment, renovation and vehicle enhancements — telehealth pods, diagnostic and telepharmacy kiosks, AI-enabled cybersecurity, clinical equipment, mobile health units, patient-transport vehicles and targeted renovations — open to rural health clinics, FQHCs, hospitals, Tribes, long-term care and local public health districts. Direct-to-state RFPs in the pipeline include Data Analytics & Outcomes Evaluation (~$2M), Project Management Support (~$1.3M), Facility Renovation Independent Verification (~$2M), a Facility/Technology Assessment (~$2.2M), workforce/care-gap needs assessments (~$2.79M), and a Ladder Payments third-party administrator (~$800K overseeing $13.72M in Year 1 incentive payments). Workforce Residency, Broadband and Pharmacy Support are core project tags; the full breakdown is in Idaho's procurement overview and budget narrative. Federal caps apply: infrastructure ≤20%, EHR replacement ≤5%, administrative ≤10%.

answers.html: Healthy Hometowns is built around restructuring rural care delivery through partnerships and hub-and-spoke networks. The centerpiece is an expansion of Governor Kim Reynolds's Centers of Excellence Program into enhanced Health Hubs — investing in telehealth, specialized equipment, provider recruitment/retention and efficient space use — alongside Communities of Care co-location of rural provider types, community health workers as system navigators, and heavy investment in chronic-disease prevention and management. Named initiatives span maternal health, cardiovascular care, cancer care, mobile integrated (EMS-led) health, high-risk OB and neonatal transport, school-based services, and a rural residency program.

Louisiana's plan is built around numbered initiatives spanning workforce, innovative and collaborative care, telehealth/access (MRAHA), and sustainable access to care. A centerpiece is a data-driven rural Medicaid Alternative Payment Model: working from a Milliman review of Medicaid claims, LDH found rural parishes run higher per-member cost but lower inpatient and readmission rates — a pattern it reads as a physical-access problem, not overutilization — and is funding a primary-care-led, provider-owned APM in response. Key project tags include Value-Based Shift, Clinical Pipeline and Rural EMS Tech.

answers.html: Michigan's award is approximately $173.1 million in Year 1 federal funds — its share of the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program (CMS assistance listing 93.798). The program is a five-year CMS cooperative agreement. The state's enacted FY2026-2027 budget carries the appropriation at $173.2 million after the legislature reduced a $250 million base by $76.8 million to align it with Michigan's actual CMS award. So far MDHHS is releasing the money as a series of themed, mid-size grant funding opportunities rather than a few large ones.

answers.html: Michigan's plan is organized as a four-part “Care Closer to Home” blueprint, built from feedback MDHHS gathered from rural providers, community partners, Medicaid beneficiaries and residents. Its pillars, reflected in the state's grant funding opportunities and subrecipient awards, are Care Closer to Home (hub-and-spoke and access, including transportation), Transforming Rural Health Through Partnerships (collaborative care integration and chronic-disease work), Workforce for Wellness (recruitment, retention and training), and Interoperability in Action (health IT and cybersecurity). The aim is to make one-time federal dollars build durable, sustainable capacity for rural providers.

Mississippi opened its first competitive phase in June 2026 with three provider grant programs making about $91.2 million available in Year 1:

  • Rural Capital Project Care Gap Closure (RCGC) — $28.5M for facility renovations, upgrades, clinic expansion and equipment; 20–30 awards of up to $3M each (excludes new construction, telehealth, cybersecurity, EHRs, and broadband).
  • Rural Provider Technology Grant (RTG) — $57M.
  • Telehealth Hub Connectivity, Equipment, and Education (TCE) — telehealth adoption.

The program continues to operate under MSDH's CMS-approved project and budget narratives without that statutory procurement overlay.

answers.html:
Eligibility runs on two tracks. Direct-to-state contracts go out as competitive RFPs (for example, the Comprehensive State Health Plan RFx), where firms bid as prime contractors. Subgrants and subawards flow to a broad pool of "Eligible Providers" — Mississippi-located hospitals (including critical access hospitals), physician practices and solo practitioners, rural health clinics, FQHCs, local health departments, Native American Sovereign Tribe healthcare facilities, certified community behavioral health clinics, SUD and dental services, and licensed long-term care facilities located in or serving rural populations. Mississippi defines "rural" as counties under 50,000 residents or fewer than 500 people per square mile, or municipalities under 15,000; an organization need not be physically rural but must show meaningful benefit to rural Mississippians. Note the state's stated preference for providers over grant-writing consultants — UEI/MAGIC vendor numbers are required only before award execution, not to apply.

Track opportunities on the MS RHTP Funding Opportunities page and the program hub.

Missouri's ToRCH Care model organizes the state into 27 Community Hub Areas, each led by a competitively selected Hub Anchor organization that convenes local providers and community partners. Underpinning it is a Digital Backbone — a foundational technology and data layer (the Missouri Integrated Health Data Fabric, or MOFAB) built on HL7 FHIR R4 and USCDI v3 standards — alongside innovative payment models, talent-pipeline development, and regional networks.

answers.html:
Montana's plan is organized around five core initiatives, with a Rural Health Center of Excellence (CoE) at its heart. The CoE is built on three objectives: a data-driven strategy that analyzes rural supply and demand at the county and facility level; long-term sustainability, helping facilities reach positive operating margins without ongoing state support; and performance incentives for facilities that opt in and hit measurable improvements. Alongside it, the state is investing in workforce recruitment, EHR/HIE modernization, EMS, and integrated care for the rural dual-eligible population.

answers.html:
Eligibility runs on two tracks, and Nevada has been unusually explicit about the line. Direct-to-state contracts go out competitively, where firms bid as prime contractors. Subawards flow to rural and frontier providers, Tribal entities, and provider-led regional consortia. Vendor rules differ by program: under RHIT, NVHA states it “will not own or operate infrastructure” and limits technology vendors, counties, academic institutions, CBOs, and school-based programs to subgrantee or fiscal-agent roles rather than prime status. Under RHOAP, by contrast, non-profits, universities, and even out-of-state and technology vendors may apply as the lead applicant if they hold a signed intent-to-contract or MOU with an eligible rural Nevada provider. “Rural” covers the 14 rural counties plus eligible rural census tracts within urban counties (verifiable via the HRSA rural eligibility tool).

Eligibility runs on two tracks. Direct-to-state contracts would go out as competitive procurements where firms bid as prime contractors. RCHI, however, flows as subawards with strict eligibility: each application needs a lead applicant — a registered 501(c)(3) not-for-profit or municipal hospital with a three-plus-year compliance history, physically present or legally domiciled in one of the eligible rural counties (the list stands at 47–49 counties across the addenda) — plus partner organizations and at least one General Hospital or Rural Emergency Hospital. Partners can sit anywhere, including out of state, as long as their work benefits eligible counties — the natural entry point for technology vendors and consultants engaging as subcontractors or implementation partners rather than direct grantees.

answers.html: Pennsylvania's federally approved application is built around six initiatives — Aging and Access, Behavioral Health, Emergency Medical Services (EMS) and Transportation, Maternal Health, Technology and Infrastructure, and Workforce. A defining bet is interoperability: the state is using RHTP dollars to move its fragmented provider base onto a single state-controlled data spine, with five certified Health Information Organizations (HIOs) feeding one statewide hub, the Pennsylvania Patient and Provider Network (P3N) — a prerequisite for care coordination, maternal-health hubs, and remote behavioral health across the plan.

answers.html: Early Year-1 money has flowed through capped payment channels tied to the six initiatives. The Rapid Response Stabilization round put $25M toward one-time purchases (supplies, equipment, renovations, structural improvements, and ambulance enhancements) at $10,000–$1,000,000 per entity. Two technology tracks then targeted interoperability: a $1.8M FQHC & FQHC Look-Alikes payment (six awards of $300,000) and a $25M EHR & HIO payment for hospitals, long-term care, home health, behavioral health, and community/ICF providers — both funding CEHRT adoption and full P3N onboarding. Recurring focuses on record include rural budget expansion, health IT, EMS, and pharmacy. The full breakdown is in DHS's federally approved RHTP application.

answers.html: The Rural Health Transformation Program was created by Section 71401 of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025) and is administered federally by CMS. To maximize its CMS merit score, West Virginia committed to specific state policy changes, including passing the Make West Virginia Healthy Act of 2026 (satisfying the CMS Presidential Fitness Test requirement), enacting a SNAP waiver prohibiting the purchase of soda with benefits, and moving to require nutrition-focused Continuing Medical Education for physicians. The state also established a statewide Advisory Panel and a specialized HealthTech panel to govern the program.

answers.html: Wisconsin's plan is focused on improving the health and wellbeing of rural communities by expanding access, improving quality, and ensuring sustainable solutions. A defining feature is its technology ambition: DHS is pursuing a single statewide electronic health records (EHR) system so rural organizations can achieve economies of scale through one procurement — a shared clinical and billing system with longitudinal records, a patient portal and a closed-loop referral network. Alongside that, the plan invests in care coordination across systems and sectors, community health workers, and rural dental efficiency and access. RHC Network, Quality Initiatives and Pharmacy Hubs are core project tags.

Wisconsin's marquee vehicle is the Rural Technology Transformation Fund:

  • Round 1 — $61M over three years, an invitation-only competition limited to the 12 FQHC organizations and 28 Rural Health Clinic organizations named in the state's Exhibit 4 (RHCs see $28M in Year 1, ~$1.01M average per org; FQHCs see $15M, ~$1.26M average).
  • Round 2 — an estimated $148M in 2027, reaching hospital systems (44), local health departments (69), Tribal clinics (14), and free/charitable and opioid-treatment facilities (26).

A separate June batch put $40M into three grants — Care Coordination (up to $10M planning), Community Health Worker ($20M), and Rural Dental Efficiency and Access ($10M). Eligible technology buys are broad and hardware-specific — EHR/IT upgrades, data-analytics subscriptions, Bluetooth blood-pressure cuffs, continuous glucose monitors, ambient AI scribes, even robotic surgical systems — within federal caps (EHR replacement 5%, administrative 8%, minor renovations 20%; no new construction).

answers.html: Wyoming's award is approximately $205.0 million in Year-1 funding, its share of the federal $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program. CMS structures the program as a five-year, spend-down initiative — a point Wyoming learned firsthand when CMS rejected the state's proposed perpetuity/endowment fund (which had aimed to stretch an anticipated ~$1 billion over five years for decades). Wyoming refiled a revised plan without the fund, which CMS approved in May 2026.

answers.html: Wyoming's plan focuses on stabilizing essential rural healthcare infrastructure rather than funding temporary programs or unneeded specialty services. Driven by the fundamentals of high fixed costs and low patient volumes across its frontier regions, the state prioritizes access to foundational care — emergency departments, reliable ambulances, and primary care — and building a durable workforce pipeline, alongside longer-term population-health investments.

answers.html:
• Emergency medical care access — roughly 48% of the budget, the largest share. Includes the “Critical Access Hospital – Basic” (CAHB) incentive rewarding small hospitals for maintaining 24/7 emergency departments, stroke/trauma imaging, and local ambulance service; EMS regionalization incentives; and “BearCare,” a public major-medical plan for residents priced out of comprehensive insurance.
  • Workforce pipeline — over 25% of the budget, funding educational support and post-graduate medical slots for physicians, nurses, and EMS personnel in exchange for five-year rural service commitments.
  • Population health — longer-term investments to improve rural health outcomes.

Recurring focuses on record include EMS stabilization, robotics, pharmacy, and high-risk care. The full breakdown is in Wyoming's approved plan.
